extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in the News of the World phone-hacking scandal and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing legal, ethical and institutional standards revealed by the News of the World phone-hacking scandal, including criminal offences, press-regulation norms, police/investigatory practice, and newsroom culture implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with criminal law and PCC code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and news organisations must operate within the criminal law and the Press Complaints Commission (PCC) code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted by Trinity Mirror in defence of staff conduct; used as an asserted baseline standard for acceptable journalism. Anti-pattern: claiming legal/PCC compliance while evidence suggests illegal methods (e.g., phone hacking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegality of intercepting communications (phone hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiring voicemail/messages or other communications without lawful authority constitutes a criminal offence (conspiracy to intercept communications / unlawful interception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of charges and convictions (e.g., convictions for intercepting voicemails, Data Protection Act breaches, and conspiracy to intercept). Examples: arrests, guilty pleas (Goodman, Mulcaire), later charges in Operation Weeting and R v Coulson, Brooks and others. Use as legal standard when assessing journalistic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data protection and unlawful acquisition of private subscriber information
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtaining or using private subscriber information and personal data in breach of the Data Protection Act (or equivalent privacy/data laws) is unlawful and subject to prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text include convictions for breaching the Data Protection Act 1998 and convictions for acquiring subscriber information from telecom databases. Relevant when evaluating investigatory methods that involve private records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and duties of legal advisers (client confidentiality and scope of advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law firms retained by news organisations are bound by client confidentiality and their engagement terms, which may limit what they can report publicly or to authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harbottle & Lewis provided 'very narrow advice' and stated they could not disclose without consent; they said they were not retained to provide a 'good conduct certificate'. Practical effect: legal advice may not absolve organisations from scrutiny; executive reliance on narrow legal opinions is an anti-pattern. Also guidance on waivers and police/parliamentary questioning of counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scope and remit for public inquiries into media practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries (e.g., the Leveson Inquiry) should examine phone hacking, initial police investigations, illicit payments to police by the press, and the broader culture and ethics of the media (including broadcasters and social media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leveson's remit as described: extend beyond newspapers to broadcasters and social media, and examine payments to police and media culture. Use as model for comprehensive inquiries into media misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic ethical standard: accuracy over speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional maxim 'Get it first. But, first, get it right.' — accuracy must not be sacrificed for scoops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited to contrast with practices that prioritised scoops obtained by unethical/illegal means. Use as a normative benchmark; anti-pattern: prioritising speed/scoops while ignoring legality and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using illegally obtained sensitive personal information
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing stories based on illegally obtained sensitive personal information (medical records, financial, legal records, private messages) is unethical and may be illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alleged acquisition/publication of medical details of Gordon Brown's infant son and illegal access to financial/phone/legal records. Use when evaluating whether a story's sourcing violated privacy or data-protection standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of corrupt or illicit payments (to police or sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments to police or other public officials for information, or illicit payments to sources, are a serious ethical and legal concern to be investigated and guarded against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leveson remit explicitly included illicit payments to police; allegations and investigations into payments feature throughout the scandal. Anti-pattern: newsrooms relying on or tolerating such payments to generate stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and oversight in police-media relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Links between police and the media require transparency; problematic relationships or preferential treatment must be examined and reformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations (e.g., Elizabeth Filkin) to extend transparency; IPCC investigations into relationships and employment arrangements (e.g., employment of Neil Wallis's daughter). Use as a criterion when assessing institutional integrity and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper handling, preservation and timely evaluation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigatory agencies must properly preserve, catalogue and evaluate evidence in a timely manner; failure to do so undermines investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism that Scotland Yard left 'boxloads' of evidence unexamined for years (kept in bin bags) is cited as an investigative failure. Use as standard for police procedure and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny of newsroom culture and editorial practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether newsroom cultures reward unethical behaviour ('do whatever it takes to get the story') including sensationalism, gossip, and manufactured controversy, rather than responsible journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes from former executives and academics accusing News Corporation of fostering a culture that prioritised scoops over ethics. Use cultural assessment to explain systemic misconduct rather than isolated 'rogue' individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate regulatory response: self-regulation vs statutory regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate criterion: whether stronger statutory regulation or stricter enforcement of self-regulation is the right response to press misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text records concerns about state regulation impinging press freedom, and criticisms of the PCC as 'toothless poodle'; some call for new independent watchdogs. Use to evaluate regulatory reform proposals, balancing press freedom and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate ethical accountability affecting investors and stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate misconduct in news organisations can and should affect investor and stakeholder actions (e.g., ethical investment divestment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church of England Ethical Investment Advisory Group withdrew investments and expressed 'no confidence' in News Corporation's return to ethical practices; cited as practical consequence and accountability lever.
